Local mirror refs/dotnet-docs/docs/fundamentals/syslib-diagnostics/syslib0060.md:35: "use ... RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes ... to create a new array with cryptographically secure bytes"; the same page's sample is "byte[] salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(saltSize);". Execution: two Hash calls on one password gave salts 7XoqLCV6ZazyxQLhBNx2ew== and BBI5LAqf/brA8kYD0MLuug==. The docs promise strength, not distinctness, which is why the claim's hedge ("not something any real run will produce") is the right wording.

refs/dotnet-docs/docs/core/whats-new/dotnet-core-2-1.md:204: "CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals* takes a fixed amount of time to return for any two inputs of the same length, which makes it suitable for use in cryptographic verification to avoid contributing to timing side-channel information." The ledger claim (time depends on length, not on where or whether they differ) is exactly this. The fixed time holds only among inputs of the same length — which is why the lesson sentence built on this claim now overshoots; see the section 4 issue.

No allowed source states PBKDF2 preimage resistance. Tried: (a) refs/dotnet-docs .../cryptographic-services.md:143 - only collision resistance ("it is computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs that hash to the same value"); (b) grep of all of refs/ for "irreversib|one-way|preimage" - no cryptography hit; (c) refs/aspnetcore-docs password-hashing.md - describes calling Pbkdf2, nothing about reversal. Nearest allowed line, CA5387, speaks of "dictionary attacks that try to guess" - guessing, not inversion. The lesson already uses round 1's suggested wording, so no new issue.

refs/dotnet-docs/docs/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/security-warnings.md:98 (CA5387): "This rule checks if a cryptographic key was generated by Rfc2898DeriveBytes with an iteration count of less than 100,000. A higher iteration count can help mitigate against dictionary attacks that try to guess the generated cryptographic key." Measured on dotnet 10, Pbkdf2 / SHA256 / 32-byte output, same salt: 10,000 iterations 10 ms; 100,000 iterations 103 ms; 1,000,000 iterations 1037 ms — proportional, as claimed.

issues.text: The clause added in round 1 overshoots claim 6 and the documentation. The mirror says the time is fixed "for any two inputs of the same length" — length is itself a property of the stored hash, so the duration does say something about it. And the whole check's duration is dominated by Pbkdf2 running the iteration count parsed out of the stored string, as the very next paragraph states ("this app's 100,000 iterations ... make slow"). "Says nothing about the stored hash" is an absolute no allowed source supports.
issues.quote: so how long the check takes says nothing about the stored hash
issues.fix: Bound it to contents: "...not on their contents — so how long the comparison takes doesn't tell anyone how much of the stored hash the typed password got right."

issues.text: "Either raw password" implies two raw passwords are in play, which contradicts the lesson's own point: only one raw password exists here (the typed one), and the stored value is not a password at all. As written, a junior can read it as "the two raw passwords are compared, just not side by side".
issues.quote: without either raw password ever sitting side by side
issues.fix: End the sentence instead with: "...anything else and the login is rejected (`E`) — the typed password is never compared against a stored password, because no stored password exists."

issues.text: Two mismatches with the block it describes. (a) The block holds four `Convert` calls — two `Convert.ToBase64String` in `Hash`, two `Convert.FromBase64String` in `Verify` — not two. (b) `HashAlgorithmName.SHA256` does not decide "which transformation runs": the transformation is PBKDF2 either way; SHA256 names the hash PBKDF2 repeats internally, and `Verify` hard-codes it instead of reading it from the stored string.
issues.quote: The algorithm name and the two `Convert` calls only decide which transformation runs and how its bytes are written as text
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "The algorithm name picks which hash `Pbkdf2` repeats inside, and the `Convert` calls on both sides only turn bytes into text and back — the salt is what this lesson turns on."

issues.text: True only of symmetric encryption. With public-key encryption the value used to encrypt is public and decrypts nothing; what recovers the plaintext is a different, private value. Stated without that condition, the sentence is a general claim about encryption that is false in a common case — and the replacement was made for readability, not accuracy.
issues.quote: whoever holds the secret value used to encrypt it can recover the original password
issues.fix: Drop the tie to encrypting: "whoever holds the secret that undoes it can recover the original password, so a leaked database plus that leaked secret means every password is exposed."

issues.text: Explanation for option d is backwards. It says the reuse-detection conclusion "would hold when every stored hash actually came from independent `Hash` calls" — that is exactly the case where it cannot hold: a fresh random salt per call means two customers with the same password get different stored strings, so matching values would essentially never appear. The key (a) is unaffected, but the feedback teaches the opposite of the lesson's point.
issues.quote: This conclusion would hold when every stored hash actually came from independent `Hash` calls — but here it doesn't
issues.fix: Rewrite d (en and vi) as: "Identical stored values could never detect reuse, not even if every row came from a real `Hash` call: a fresh random salt per call means two customers with the same password still get different stored strings. These two rows match because one `UPDATE` wrote one literal value into both."

issues.text: Explanation for option b rebuts something b no longer says. Since the round-1 rewrite, b infers "`Hash` must have used the same salt and iteration count both times" — a sound inference from identical output, not an error. The actual error in b is its premise that `Hash` produced these rows at all. The explanation attacks a fixed-salt implementation instead, so a learner who reasoned correctly is told the reasoning was wrong.
issues.quote: This would hold when `Hash` used a fixed salt every time, the way a plain, unsalted hash function does
issues.fix: Rewrite b (en and vi) as: "Identical output would indeed mean the same salt — but nothing here says `Hash` produced these rows. It never ran for them: one migration `UPDATE` wrote the same literal string into both, so the values say nothing about the passwords."

issues.text: The key (c) is correct given the lesson, but the rewritten wording reintroduces the absolute the round-1 review took out of sections 4 and 6. Claim 7 is `unverified`: no allowed source says a hash cannot be turned back; what is supportable is that nothing computes the password back, leaving guessing. "Nothing turns a hash back into anything" also over-claims beyond passwords.
issues.quote: while nothing turns a hash back into anything
issues.fix: Rewrite option c (en and vi) as: "False, because someone holding the encryption secret can turn ciphertext back into the original password, while nothing computes a password back out of a hash — the only route is guessing." Align the `correct` explanation the same way.

issues.text: Explanation for the new option d never names d's main falsehood: it claims "Neither method is called anywhere", while `Verify` is called from `AuthController.Login` — the fact the key rests on. The explanation also says the migration's SQL "is generated from that code", which is loose for `migrationBuilder.Sql(...)`: that string is written out literally by the developer and EF Core only issues it.
issues.quote: the SQL it issues is generated from that code, not typed by hand into the database
issues.fix: Rewrite d (en and vi) as: "`Verify` is called — from `AuthController.Login` — so 'neither method' is already wrong. And the hashes weren't typed into the database by hand either: the migration is C# that EF Core runs, carrying that literal string in its `Sql(...)` statement."

issues.text: I can see what this line does but not why it is in the lesson. Nothing says why the duration of a comparison would matter, so the sentence is a fact with no consequence — I read it twice and then skipped it. Afterwards I am unsure why `==` would be wrong, which I need when the quiz asks me to place the `FixedTimeEquals` step.
issues.quote: The comparison itself uses `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, not `==` — a comparison whose duration depends on the length of the two byte sequences, not on their contents.
issues.fix: After 'not on their contents', add one clause giving the point: '— so how long the check takes says nothing about the stored hash.'

issues.text: `Pbkdf2` is node B of the diagram and appears twice in the prose, but nothing ever says what it is: a library, an algorithm, a class of my own? issues.quote: runs `Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2` again on the password just typed, using that same salt and iteration count
issues.fix: Gloss it inline with words already in Core concepts: 'runs `Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2` — the one-way transformation itself — again on the password just typed'.
